title: "Defining random variables"

The [preceding page](why-random-variables.qmd) introduced a random variable as a function from complete outcomes to values. But not every function between arbitrary measurable spaces automatically supports probability statements. What property must the mapping have? We now add the measurability condition that answers this question.

We continue with the [prepared CMUdict pronunciation table introduced on the preceding page](why-random-variables.qmd#the-pronunciation-entry-outcomes). Let $V$ map each pronunciation entry to its number of vowel phones.

We distinguish the outcome and value spaces, work backward from value sets through preimages, and then state the measurability condition that makes the induced probability statements available.

```{r}
#| label: load-cmudict-definition
library(ggplot2)

cmu <- read.csv(
  "data/cmudict/cmudict-pronunciations.csv",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE,
  check.names = FALSE,
  na.strings = ""
)
cmu$outcome_id <- seq_len(nrow(cmu))

stopifnot(
  nrow(cmu) == 133854L,
  !anyDuplicated(cmu$entry),
  all(cmu$vowel_phone_count >= 1L),
  !anyNA(cmu$vowel_phone_count)
)
```

## Distinguishing the two spaces

Let $\langle\Omega,\mathcal F\rangle$ be the measurable space of pronunciation-entry outcomes, using the [event space introduced earlier](../foundations/event-spaces.qmd). Let $\langle\mathcal X,\mathcal G\rangle$ be the measurable space of nonnegative integer counts. The function has the form

$$
V:\Omega\longrightarrow\mathcal X.
$$

The set $\mathcal X$ is the declared codomain of $V$, written $\operatorname{cod}(V)$. A statement such as $v\in\operatorname{cod}(V)$ refers to the declared value space. It does not mean that $v$ appeared in the observed resource, and it does not require that $v$ have positive probability.

For current purposes, we take

$$
\mathcal X\equiv\mathbb Z_{\geq0}
$$

and let $\mathcal G$ contain all subsets of $\mathcal X$. This codomain includes counts absent from the prepared lexicon.

## Working backward with a preimage

We use the observed median vowel-phone count to define a set in the value space.

```{r}
#| label: cmudict-preimage
median_vowels <- unname(quantile(cmu$vowel_phone_count, 0.5, type = 1))
median_preimage <- subset(
  cmu,
  vowel_phone_count == median_vowels,
  select = c(outcome_id, entry, phones, vowel_phone_count)
)
at_most_median_preimage <- subset(
  cmu,
  vowel_phone_count <= median_vowels,
  select = c(outcome_id, entry, phones, vowel_phone_count)
)

stopifnot(
  nrow(median_preimage) == sum(cmu$vowel_phone_count == median_vowels),
  nrow(at_most_median_preimage) ==
    sum(cmu$vowel_phone_count <= median_vowels)
)

head(median_preimage)
```

Before writing notation, state the operation in words: collect every pronunciation entry whose vowel-phone count equals the empirical median. The result is

$$
V^{-1}(\{q_{.5}\})
\equiv
\{\omega\in\Omega\mid V(\omega)\in\{q_{.5}\}\}.
$$

This set is the [**preimage**](https://stats.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Probability_Theory/Probability_Mathematical_Statistics_and_Stochastic_Processes_%28Siegrist%29/02%3A_Probability_Spaces/2.09%3A_Probability_Spaces_Revisited) of $\{q_{.5}\}$ under $V$. Here $q_{.5}$ is `r median_vowels`, and the preimage contains `r format(nrow(median_preimage), big.mark = ",")` entries.

The superscript $-1$ does not say that $V$ has an inverse function. Many pronunciation entries map to the same vowel count, so the count cannot recover one unique entry. The preimage collects all of them.

```{r}
#| label: plot-cmudict-preimage
#| fig-cap: "Empirical vowel-phone counts. The accent bar marks the value whose preimage is inspected above."
vowel_counts <- as.data.frame(table(cmu$vowel_phone_count))
names(vowel_counts) <- c("vowel_phone_count", "entries")
vowel_counts$vowel_phone_count <- as.integer(as.character(vowel_counts$vowel_phone_count))
vowel_counts$selected <- vowel_counts$vowel_phone_count == median_vowels

ggplot(vowel_counts, aes(vowel_phone_count, entries, fill = selected)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.8) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = "grey", `TRUE` = "steelblue"),
                    guide = "none") +
  labs(x = "Vowel phones in pronunciation", y = "Pronunciation entries") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)
```

## Stating measurability

The function $V$ is a random variable when

$$
E\in\mathcal G
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
V^{-1}(E)\in\mathcal F.
$$

This condition is called [**measurability**](https://stats.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Probability_Theory/Probability_Mathematical_Statistics_and_Stochastic_Processes_%28Siegrist%29/02%3A_Probability_Spaces/2.09%3A_Probability_Spaces_Revisited). It says that every measurable question about the value corresponds to a measurable event in the original outcome space.

If $\{q_{.5}\}\in\mathcal G$, then the set of pronunciation entries in its preimage must belong to $\mathcal F$. Otherwise the expression “the probability that a pronunciation has the median vowel count” would refer to an event to which the model assigns no probability.

In this finite empirical model, $\mathcal F\equiv2^\Omega$, so every preimage is measurable because every subset of pronunciation entries belongs to $\mathcal F$. The requirement becomes more substantive for larger outcome spaces, but its interpretation remains the same.

Here is a finite case in which measurability fails. Let
$\Omega=\{\omega_1,\omega_2\}$ but choose
$\mathcal F=\{\varnothing,\Omega\}$, so the model cannot distinguish the two
outcomes. If $V(\omega_1)=0$ and $V(\omega_2)=1$, then
$V^{-1}(\{0\})=\{\omega_1\}\notin\mathcal F$. The mapping asks a value-level
question that the outcome event space cannot measure, so it is not a random
variable between these measurable spaces.

The full chain is:

$$
\text{value set }E
\ \xrightarrow{\ V^{-1}\ }\
\text{outcome event }V^{-1}(E)
\ \xrightarrow{\ \mathbb{P}\ }\
\text{probability }\mathbb{P}(V\in E).
$$

## Reading probability notation through the preimage

Once $V$ is defined, probability notation for its values is shorthand:

$$
\mathbb{P}(V=q_{.5})
\equiv
\mathbb{P}\bigl(V^{-1}(\{q_{.5}\})\bigr).
$$

Similarly,

$$
\mathbb{P}(V\leq q_{.5})
$$

means the probability of the preimage of all values at or below the median. The probability measure still acts on an event of outcomes.

## Check your understanding

1. Use `cmu` to compute $V^{-1}(\{1\})$. How many pronunciation entries does it contain?
2. Why is a preimage a set of pronunciation entries rather than a set of vowel counts?
3. State the measurability condition in words.
4. Use `at_most_median_preimage` to compute the empirical probability $\mathbb{P}(V\leq q_{.5})$.
5. In the two-outcome counterexample, would enlarging $\mathcal F$ to
   $2^\Omega$ make $V$ measurable? Why?

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. $V^{-1}(\{1\})$ contains the 16,935 pronunciation-entry outcomes with exactly one vowel phone. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
2. A preimage is a subset of the domain, so its members are pronunciation entries mapped to one rather than the output value one itself. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
3. Measurability requires the preimage of every measurable set of output values to be a measurable event in the pronunciation-entry space. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
4. The empirical probability is $\mathbb{P}(V\leq q_{.5})=(16{,}935+61{,}493)/133{,}854=0.585922$. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
5. Yes. The power set contains both singleton preimages, and thus the preimage
   of every subset of the value space.

</details>

A value event is pulled back through a random variable to an outcome event.
Measurability requires that preimage to belong to $\mathcal F$, because the
probability measure still acts on outcomes. The [next
page](discrete-random-variables.qmd) considers variables whose possible values
can be listed.
